paragraphs.translation: 2.3 Algorithmic Problems 25 If there exists an algorithm for a language L that recognizes L, we will say that L is recursive. We frequently use a language L ⊆ Σ∗ to specify a certain property of words from Σ∗ (or of objects represented by the words). The words that are in L have this property, and all words from L∁ = Σ∗ − L do not have this property. Typically, we represent a decision problem (Σ, L) as follows: Input: x ∈ Σ∗. Output: A(x) ∈ Σbool = {0, 1}, where A(x) = { 1, if x ∈ L (Yes, x has the property), 0, if x ∉ L (No, x does not have the property). For example, ({a, b}, {a^n b^n | n ∈ N}) is a decision problem that can also be represented as follows: Input: x ∈ {a, b}∗. Output: Yes, if x = a^n b^n for some n ∈ N. No, otherwise. Example 2.2. A well-known and practically important decision problem is the primality test (Σbool, {x ∈ (Σbool)∗ | number(x) is a prime number}). The usual representation is Input: x ∈ (Σbool)∗. Output: Yes, if number(x) is a prime number. No, otherwise. ♦ Example 2.3. Let L = {x ∈ (ΣKeyboard)∗ | x is a syntactically correct program in C++}. We can consider the following problem, which is a subtask of the compiler. Input: x ∈ (ΣKeyboard)∗. Output: Yes, if x ∈ L. No, otherwise. ♦ Example 2.4. The Hamiltonian cycle problem (HC) is (Σ, HC), where Σ = {0, 1, #} and HC = {x ∈ Σ∗ | x encodes an undirected graph that contains a Hamiltonian cycle. 4}. ♦ Recursion is an important concept and therefore we will later provide a formally precise definition of this concept with the formal model of computation of a Turing machine. 4For the record: A Hamiltonian cycle of a graph G is a closed path (cycle) that visits every node of G exactly once.

paragraphs.translation: 26 2 Alphabets, Words, Languages, and the Representation of Problems Example 2.5. The satisfiability problem of propositional logic formulas (SAT) is (Σlogic, SAT) with SAT = {x ∈ (Σlogic)∗ | x encodes a satisfiable Boolean formula}. ♦ An important subclass of decision problems is the class of equivalence problems. The equivalence problem for programs, for example, consists of deciding whether two programs A and B in some fixed programming language (i.e., for the input (A, B) ∈ (ΣKeyboard)∗) are equivalent. Another example is to decide whether two Boolean formulas represent the same Boolean function. Definition 2.12. Let Σ and Γ be two alphabets. We say that an algorithm A computes a function (transformation) f :Σ ∗ → Γ∗ if A(x) = f(x) for all x ∈ Σ∗. Decision problems are special cases of function computations because solving a decision problem means computing the characteristic function of a language. At first glance, one might get the impression that computing functions is the most general representation of algorithmic problems. The following definition shows that this is not the case. Definition 2.13. Let Σ and Γ be two alphabets, and let R ⊆ Σ∗ × Γ∗ be a relation in Σ∗ and Γ∗. An algorithm A computes R (or solves the relation problem R) if, for every x ∈ Σ∗ for which there exists a y ∈ Γ∗ with (x, y) ∈ R, it holds that (x, A(x)) ∈ R. Note that it is sufficient to find one of potentially infinitely many y with (x, y) ∈ R for each given x to solve a relation problem. The following examples demonstrate that relation problems are not only a mathematical generalization of function computation but that we have many such problems in practice. Let Rfac ⊆ (Σbool)∗ × (Σbool)∗, where (x, y) ∈ Rfac if and only if either Number(y) is a factor of Number(x), or y = 1 if Number(x) is a prime number, or y = 0 if x ∈ {0, 1}. A visual representation of this relation problem could look as follows. Input: x ∈ (Σbool)∗. Output: y ∈ (Σbool)∗, where Number(y) = ⎧ ⎪⎪⎨ ⎪⎪⎩ 0, if x = 0 or x = 1, 1, if x is a prime number, k, otherwise, where k is a factor of Number(x). The characteristic function fL of a language L ⊆ Σ∗ is a function from Σ ∗ to {0, 1} with fL(x) = 1 if and only if x ∈ L. A number a is a factor of a number b if a divides b and a ∉ {1, b}.

paragraphs.text: 2.3 Algorithmische Probleme 27 Ein anderes schweres Problem ist die Beweiserstellung. Es sei RBeweis ⊆ (ΣTastatur)∗ × (ΣTastatur)∗, wobei ( x, y) ∈ RBeweis,w e n ne n t w e d e rx eine wahre Aussage in einer be- stimmten mathematischen Theorie kodiert und y einen Beweis der durch x kodierten Aussage darstellt oder y = ␣,w e n nxkeine wahre Aussage darstellt. Für uns sind aber die Optimierungsprobleme, die einen Spezialfall von Relationsproble- men darstellen, von zentralem Interesse. Um die Struktur von Optimierungsproblemen anschaulich darzustellen, benutzen wir folgende Beschreibung statt der Relationsdarstel- lung. Informell bestimmt eine Eingabe x eines Optimierungsproblems eine Menge M(x) zulässiger Lösungen für x. Damit bekommen wir auch eine Relation R mit (x, y) ∈ R, wenn y eine zulässige Lösung von x ist. Aber dieses R ist nicht das zu lösende Rela- tionsproblem. Die Eingabe x bestimmt zusätzlich noch den Preis für jedes y mit der Eigenschaft (x, y) ∈ R. Die Ausgabe zu x muss eine zulässige Lösung mit dem günstigsten (je nach Aufgabenspeziﬁzierung minimalen oder maximalen) Preis sein. Deﬁnition 2.14. Ein Optimierungsproblem ist ein 6-Tupel U =( ΣI , ΣO,L ,M, cost, goal), wobei: (i) ΣI ist ein Alphabet (genannt Eingabealphabet), (ii) ΣO ist ein Alphabet (genannt Ausgabealphabet), (iii) L ⊆ Σ∗I ist die Sprache der zulässigen Eingaben (als Eingaben kommen nur Wör- ter in Frage, die eine sinnvolle Bedeutung haben ).E i nx ∈ L wird ein Problemfall (Instanz) von U genannt. (iv) M ist eine Funktion von L nach P(Σ∗O), und für jedes x ∈ L ist M(x) die Menge der zulässigen Lösungen für x, (v) cost ist eine Funktion, cost: ⋃x∈L(M(x)×{x}) → R+, genannt Kostenfunktion, (vi) goal ∈{ Minimum, Maximum} ist das Optimierungsziel. Eine zulässige Lösung α ∈M (x) heißt optimal für den Problemfall x des Optimie- rungsproblems U, falls cost(α, x)= Opt U (x) = goal{cost(β,x ) | β ∈M (x)}. Ein Algorithmus A löst U, falls für jedes x ∈ L (i) A(x) ∈M (x), {A(x) ist eine zulässige Lösung des Problemfalls x von U.} (ii) cost(A(x),x ) = goal{cost(β,x ) | β ∈M (x)}. Fal lsgoal = Minimum, ist U ein Minimierungsproblem; falls goal = Maximum, ist U ein Maximierungsproblem.
paragraphs.translation: 2.3 Algorithmic Problems 27 Another difficult problem is proof generation. Let RProof ⊆ (ΣKeyboard)∗ × (ΣKeyboard)∗, where (x, y) ∈ RProof if x encodes a true statement in a given mathematical theory and y represents a proof of the statement encoded by x, or y = ␣ if x does not represent a true statement. However, we are primarily interested in optimization problems, which represent a special case of relational problems. To illustrate the structure of optimization problems, we use the following description instead of the relational representation. Informally, an input x of an optimization problem determines a set M(x) of feasible solutions for x. This also gives us a relation R with (x, y) ∈ R if y is a feasible solution of x. But this R is not the relational problem to be solved. The input x additionally specifies the cost for each y with the property (x, y) ∈ R. The output for x must be a feasible solution with the lowest (depending on the problem specification, minimal or maximal) cost. Definition 2.14. An optimization problem is a 6-tuple U = (ΣI, ΣO, L, M, cost, goal), where: (i) ΣI is an alphabet (called input alphabet), (ii) ΣO is an alphabet (called output alphabet), (iii) L ⊆ Σ∗I is the language of feasible inputs (as inputs, only words that have meaningful significance are considered). An x ∈ L is called a problem instance of U. (iv) M is a function from L to P(Σ∗O), and for each x ∈ L, M(x) is the set of feasible solutions for x, (v) cost is a function, cost: ⋃x∈L(M(x)×{x}) → R+, called the cost function, (vi) goal ∈ {Minimum, Maximum} is the optimization objective. A feasible solution α ∈ M(x) is called optimal for the problem case x of the optimization problem U if cost(α, x) = OptU(x) = goal{cost(β, x) | β ∈ M(x)}. An algorithm A solves U if for every x ∈ L, (i) A(x) ∈ M(x), {A(x) is a feasible solution of the problem case x of U.} (ii) cost(A(x), x) = goal{cost(β, x) | β ∈ M(x)}. If goal = Minimum, U is a minimization problem; if goal = Maximum, U is a maximization problem.

paragraphs.text: 28 2 Alphabete, Wörter, Sprachen und die Darstellung von Problemen In der Deﬁnition eines Optimierungsproblems als 6-Tupel hat das Eingabealphabet Σ I die gleiche Bedeutung wie das Alphabet von Entscheidungsproblemen, d. h., Σ I benutzt man, um die Instanzen von U darzustellen. Analog benutzt man das Ausgabealphabet ΣO für die Darstellung von Ausgaben (zulässigen Lösungen). Die Sprache L ⊆ Σ∗I ist die Menge der Darstellungen von Problemfällen. Dies bedeutet, dass wir uns auf das Optimierungsproblem und nicht auf das Entscheidungsproblem (Σ I ,L ) konzentrieren und dass wir voraussetzen, dass eine Eingabe aus Σ ∗I − L nie vorkommen wird. Ein Problemfall x ∈ L formuliert meistens eine Menge von Einschränkungen und M(x) ist die Menge von Objekten (zulässigen Lösungen zu x), die diese Einschränkungen erfüllen. In der Regel bestimmt der Problemfall x auch, wie hoch die Kosten cost(α, x) für jedes α ∈M (x) sind. Die Aufgabe ist, in der Menge der zulässigen Lösungen M(x) zu x eine optimale zu ﬁnden. Die typische Schwierigkeit ist, dass die Menge M(x) eine so große Mächtigkeit hat, dass es unmöglich ist, alle zulässigen Lösungen aus M(x)z u generieren und deren Kosten zu vergleichen. Um die Speziﬁkation konkreter Optimierungsprobleme zu veranschaulichen, lassen wir oft die Speziﬁkation von Σ I ,Σ O und die Darstellung von Daten über Σ I und ΣO aus. Wir setzen einfach voraus, dass die typischen Daten wie Zahlen, Graphen oder Formeln in der oben präsentierten Darstellung vorkommen. Dadurch reduzieren wir die Deﬁnition eines Optimierungsproblems auf die Speziﬁkation folgender vier Objekte: • die Menge der Problemfälle L, also die zulässigen Eingaben, • die Menge der Einschränkungen, gegeben durch jeden Problemfall x ∈ L, und damit M(x) für jedes x ∈ L, • die Kostenfunktion, • das Optimierungsziel. Beispiel 2.6. Das Traveling-Salesman-Problem (TSP). Die Aufgabe besteht darin, in einem gegebenen kantengewichteten, vollständigen Graphen einen Hamiltonschen Kreis mit minimalen Kosten zu ﬁnden. Eingabe: Ein kantengewichteter vollständiger Graph (G, c), wobei G =( V,E ), V = {v1,...,v n} für ein n ∈ N −{ 0}, und c: E → N −{ 0}. {Strikt formal ist die Eingabe jedes Wort x ∈{ 0, 1, #}∗, so dass x einen gewichteten, vollständigen Graphen (G, c) darstellt} Einschränkungen: Für jeden Problemfall (G, c)i s tM(G, c) die Menge aller Hamil- tonschen Kreise von G. Jeder Hamiltonsche Kreis lässt sich durch ein ( n +1 ) - T u p e l von Knoten vi1 ,v i2 ,...,v in ,v i1 darstellen, wobei (i1,...,i n) eine Permutation von {1, 2,...,n } ist. Man beachte, dass diese Darstellung nicht eindeutig ist. {Eine streng formale Darstellung von M(G, c) wäre die Menge aller Wörter y1#y2# ... #yn ∈{ 0, 1, #}∗ =Σ ∗O mit yi ∈{ 0, 1}+ für i =1 , 2,...,n und {Nummer(y1), Nummer(y2),..., Nummer(yn)} = {1, 2,...,n }} Kosten: Für jeden Hamiltonschen Kreis H = vi1 ,v i2 ,...,v in ,v i1 ∈M (G, c)i s t cost((vi1 ,...,v in ,v i1 ), (G, c)) = n∑ j=1 c({vij ,v i(j mod n)+1}),
paragraphs.translation: 28 2 Alphabets, Words, Languages, and the Representation of Problems In the definition of an optimization problem as a 6-tuple, the input alphabet Σ I has the same meaning as the alphabet of decision problems, i.e., Σ I is used to represent the instances of U. Similarly, the output alphabet Σ O is used for the representation of outputs (feasible solutions). The language L ⊆ Σ∗ I is the set of representations of problem instances. This means that we focus on the optimization problem and not on the decision problem (Σ I ,L ), and we assume that an input from Σ ∗ I − L will never occur. A problem instance x ∈ L typically formulates a set of constraints, and M(x) is the set of objects (feasible solutions to x) that satisfy these constraints. Generally, the problem instance x also determines the cost cost(α, x) for each α ∈ M(x). The task is to find an optimal solution in the set of feasible solutions M(x) for x. The typical difficulty is that the set M(x) has such a large cardinality that it is impossible to generate all feasible solutions from M(x) and compare their costs. To illustrate the specification of concrete optimization problems, we often omit the specification of Σ I , Σ O and the representation of data over Σ I and Σ O. We simply assume that typical data such as numbers, graphs, or formulas are present in the representation presented above. This reduces the definition of an optimization problem to the specification of the following four objects: • the set of problem instances L, i.e., the feasible inputs, • the set of constraints given by each problem instance x ∈ L, and thus M(x) for each x ∈ L, • the cost function, • the optimization objective. Example 2.6. The Traveling Salesman Problem (TSP). The task is to find a Hamiltonian cycle with minimal costs in a given edge-weighted, complete graph. Input: An edge-weighted complete graph (G, c), where G = (V, E), V = {v1,...,v n} for n ∈ N −{ 0}, and c: E → N −{ 0}. {Strictly formally, the input is any word x ∈{ 0, 1, #}∗, such that x represents a weighted, complete graph (G, c)} Constraints: For each problem instance (G, c), M(G, c) is the set of all Hamiltonian cycles of G. Each Hamiltonian cycle can be represented by a (n + 1)-tuple of nodes v i1 , v i2 , ..., v in , v i1 , where (i1,...,i n) is a permutation of {1, 2,...,n}. Note that this representation is not unique. {A strictly formal representation of M(G, c) would be the set of all words y 1#y 2#...#y n ∈{ 0, 1, #}∗ = Σ∗ O with y i ∈{ 0, 1}+ for i = 1, 2,...,n and {Number(y1), Number(y2),..., Number(yn)} = {1, 2,...,n}} Costs: For every Hamiltonian cycle H = v i1 , v i2 ,..., v in , v i1 ∈ M(G, c), it holds that cost((v i1 ,..., v in , v i1 ), (G, c)) = n∑ j=1 c({v ij , v i(j mod n)+1}),

In der Anwendung erscheinen aber oft nur Problemfälle, die gewisse gute Eigenschaften haben und für die man bei der Suche nach einer guten Lösung bessere Chancen hat. Wir sagen, dass ein Optimierungs- problem U1 =( ΣI , ΣO,L ′,M, cost, goal)e i n Teilproblem des Optimierungsproblems U2 =( ΣI , ΣO,L ,M, cost, goal) ist, falls L′ ⊆ L ist. Auf diese Weise deﬁnieren wir auch das metrische TSP (Δ-TSP) als ein Teilproblem von TSP. Das bedeutet, dass die Einschränkungen, die Kosten und das Ziel genauso deﬁniert sind wie bei TSP, nur die Menge der Eingaben (Problemfälle) wird folgendermaßen eingeschränkt: Jeder Problemfall (G, c) von Δ-TSP erfüllt die sogenannte Dreiecksungleichung, was bedeutet, dass c({u, v}) ≤ c({u, w})+c({w, v }) für alle Knoten u, v, w von G. Dies ist eine natürliche Eigenschaft, die besagt, dass die direkte Verbindung zwischen u und v nicht teurer sein darf als beliebige Umwege (Verbindungen über andere Knoten). Objective: Minimum. For the instance of TSP from Figure 2.4, it holds that cost((v1, v2, v3, v4, v5, v1), (G, c)) = 8+1+7+2+1=19, cost((v1, v5, v3, v2, v4, v1), (G, c)) = 1+1+1+1+1=5. The Hamiltonian cycle v1, v5, v3, v2, v4, v1 is the only optimal solution for this instance of TSP. ♦ The TSP is a hard optimization problem. However, in application, often only instances emerge that have certain good properties, and for which one has better chances of finding a good solution. We say that an optimization problem U1 = (ΣI, ΣO, L′, M, cost, goal) is a subproblem of the optimization problem U2 = (ΣI, ΣO, L, M, cost, goal) if L′ ⊆ L. In this way, we also define the metric TSP (Δ-TSP) as a subproblem of TSP. This means that the constraints, costs, and goals are defined the same way as in TSP; only the set of inputs (instances) is restricted as follows: each instance (G, c) of Δ-TSP satisfies the so-called triangle inequality, which means that c({u, v}) ≤ c({u, w}) + c({w, v}) for all nodes u, v, w of G. This is a natural property that states that the direct connection between u and v must not be more expensive than any detours (connections through other nodes). paragraphs.translation: 1.3 For the Students 9 This book is dedicated to certain parts of theoretical computer science. Why is the study of theoretical computer science considered difficult? There is no easy path to a deeper understanding and mastery of methods that have impressive applications. This should not surprise anyone. If someone wants to run 100 meters in under 10 seconds or jump over 8 meters, they must also undergo many years of quite rigorous training. Whenever one wants to achieve something special, one must also do something special for it. Learning a science is no exception, and perhaps you additionally face the motivational difficulty that you cannot yet clearly see the goal during your efforts and cannot assess its value. Thus, a lot of endurance is required, and especially the willingness to iterate over each topic many times to develop a deeper understanding of the interconnections. This book is intended to ease your introduction to the algorithmic parts of theoretical computer science. For this purpose, we use the following three concepts: 1. Simplicity and Clarity We explain everything that can be simply explained, simply. We avoid unnecessary mathematical abstractions; we strive to be as concrete as possible. In doing so, we create an entry point with elementary knowledge of mathematics. In all more complicated considerations and proofs, we first explain the relationships and ideas in a clear and informal way before moving on to formal justifications. At the points marked with *, we recommend that technical college students and non-computer scientists skip the formal proofs. Moreover, these groups can, for example, forgo the technical handling of the formal model of the Turing machine in the computability section, and achieve an understanding of the fundamentals of the theory of computability through argumentation at the level of programs (in any programming language). Clarity is more important to us than the presentation of the best-known results. If we can explain the methods and proof ideas more easily with weaker results, then we prefer to present such results to the technical and opaque presentation of stronger results. Throughout the book, we follow the approach of gradually stepping from the simple to the complex and thereby avoid leaps in thought. 2. "Less is sometimes more" or a context-sensitive presentation Many curricula and textbooks start from the mistaken conception that they must primarily provide the reader with a certain quantity of information. In lectures or in teaching materials, one then plays a false optimization game—aiming to convey as much knowledge and results as possible in minimal time. This often results in the presentation of a large amount of individual results that appear too isolated. In doing so, the context of the whole event is lost. The philosophy of this book is different. We want to shape the thinking of the students. Therefore, the number of presented results is not as important to us. We focus on the historical development of computer science concepts and ways of thinking, and the presentation of definitions, results, proofs, and methods is only a means to achieve this goal. Therefore, we willingly accept the reduction.

paragraphs.translation: 14 2 Alphabets, Words, Languages, and the Representation of Problems An important point is that Kolmogorov complexity is a valuable tool for studying computations, as will be made clear at several points in this book. 2.2 Alphabets, Words, and Languages In algorithmic data processing, we represent data and the objects we consider through sequences of symbols. Just like in the development of natural languages, we start by defining the symbols we want to use to represent the data. Below, N = {0, 1, 2,... } denotes the set of natural numbers. Definition 2.1. A finite non-empty set Σ is called an alphabet. The elements of an alphabet are called letters (characters, symbols). The meaning is the same as in natural languages: The alphabet is used to create a written representation of a language. It is only important for us to know that we can choose any, but only finitely many symbols, to realize a representation of the objects under study. We now present some of the most frequently used alphabets here. • Σbool = {0, 1} is the Boolean alphabet with which computers operate. • Σlat = {a, b, c, . . . , z} is the Latin alphabet. • ΣTastatur = Σlat ∪ {A, B, ..., Z, ␣, >, <, (, ), ..., !} is the alphabet of all symbols on the computer keyboard, where ␣ is the space symbol. • Σm = {0, 1, 2,..., m − 1} for any m ≥ 1 is an alphabet for the m-ary representation of numbers. • Σlogic = {0, 1, x, (, ), ∧, ∨, ¬} is an alphabet that allows for a good representation of Boolean formulas. We now define words as sequences of letters. Note that the term 'word' in computer science refers to any text and not just the meaning of the term 'word' in natural languages. Definition 2.2. Let Σ be an alphabet. A word over Σ is a finite (possibly empty) sequence of letters from Σ. The empty word λ is the empty sequence of letters. (Sometimes ε is used instead of λ.) The length |w| of a word w is the length of the word as a sequence, i.e., the number of occurrences of letters in w. Σ∗ is the set of all words over Σ, and Σ+ = Σ ∗ − {λ}. The sequence 0, 1, 0, 0, 1, 1 is a word over Σbool and over ΣTastatur, with |0, 1, 0, 0, 1, 1| = 6. The empty word λ is a word over any alphabet, with |λ| = 0.

Wir setzen voraus, dass der Leser weiß, was ein Programm ist. In welcher Programmiersprache es geschrieben ist, spielt hier keine Rolle. Wenn wir Programme als Algorithmen betrachten, fordern wir jedoch, dass ein solches Programm für jede zulässige Eingabe hält und eine Ausgabe liefert. Daher ist es für einen Algorithmus unzulässig, in eine Endlosschleife zu laufen. Mit dieser Voraussetzung realisiert ein Programm (Algorithmus) A typischerweise eine Abbildung A:Σ ∗1 → Σ∗2 für irgendwelche Alphabete Σ1 und Σ2. Dies bedeutet, dass (i) die Eingaben als Wörter kodiert sind, (ii) die Ausgaben als Wörter kodiert sind und (iii) A für jede Eingabe eine eindeutige Ausgabe bestimmt. Für jeden Algorithmus A und jede Eingabe x bezeichnen wir mit A(x) die Ausgabe des Algorithmus A für die Eingabe x. Wir sagen, dass zwei Algorithmen (Programme) A und B äquivalent sind, falls beide über dem gleichen Eingabealphabet Σ arbeiten und A(x)= B(x) für alle x ∈ Σ∗. Prove or disprove the following statement: h(L1)h(L2) = h(L1L2). 2.3 Algorithmic Problems Before we formally define the intuitive concept of an algorithm using the model of Turing machines, we will use the term program instead of algorithm. We assume that the reader knows what a program is. The programming language in which it is written does not matter here. However, when we consider programs as algorithms, we require that such a program halts and produces an output for every permissible input. Therefore, it is unacceptable for an algorithm to enter an infinite loop. With this requirement, a program (algorithm) A typically implements a mapping A: Σ∗1 → Σ∗2 for any alphabets Σ1 and Σ2. This means that (i) the inputs are encoded as words, (ii) the outputs are encoded as words, and (iii) A determines a unique output for each input. For every algorithm A and every input x, we denote the output of algorithm A for input x as A(x). We say that two algorithms (programs) A and B are equivalent if they operate over the same input alphabet Σ and A(x) = B(x) for all x ∈ Σ∗. Below, we present some basic classes of algorithmic problems. We start with decision problems, which are commonly used to build the theory of computability and complexity theory. Definition 2.11. The decision problem (Σ, L) for a given alphabet Σ and a given language L ⊆ Σ∗ is to decide, for every x ∈ Σ∗, whether x ∈ L or x ∉ L. An algorithm A solves the decision problem (Σ, L) if for all x ∈ Σ∗ it holds that: A(x) = { 1, if x ∈ L, 0, if x ∉ L. We also say that A recognizes the language L.
